documents.unit: Emory College of Arts and Sciences (Academic Affairs and Faculty Partnerships)
documents.title: Emory College Syllabus Additions (AI statement)
documents.stance_why: The document says "It is up to the instructor to determine whether student use of Artificial Intelligence is allowed", so it sets no college-wide stance and hands the decision to instructors. The only template offered is a no-AI one, but it is optional ('you may use') and 'adapt as needed', so there are no tiers.
documents.summary: A College syllabus-additions sheet telling instructors what to paste into syllabi. Its AI section leaves the decision to each instructor, asks for a syllabus statement on AI, and supplies a no-AI template that frames unauthorized AI use as plagiarism and an Honor Code violation.

units.why: The sentence says "It is up to the instructor to determine" whether AI is allowed, so the rule is delegated per instructor and per assignment; this is P04, the stance-setting type, not P09 which concerns the statement itself.
units.anchor: It is up to the instructor to determine whether student use of
units.frag_start: It is up to the instructor
units.policy: It is up to the instructor to determine whether student use of Artificial Intelligence is allowed for any assignments.

units.why: "The syllabus should include a statement" on AI use is a recommended duty addressed to instructors, matching P09 (state AI expectations in the syllabus or assignment instructions).
units.anchor: The syllabus should include a statement that addresses the extent to which AI use
units.frag_start: The syllabus should include a statement
units.policy: The syllabus should include a statement that addresses the extent to which AI use is appropriate for the course and/or any specific assignments.

units.why: The statement "may be included as part of the Honor Code statement for the course or listed as its own course policy" is a permission about where the AI statement goes; it fits P09 (syllabus AI statement) better than P04 because it concerns communication format, not who decides.
units.anchor: may be included as part of the Honor Code statement for the course
units.frag_start: This may be included as part

units.why: The suggested language bars using AI "to generate any content for any assignment in this course", a default no-AI rule for graded work, so P01; the misconduct label is coded separately as P36.
units.anchor: Using an artificial intelligence program to generate any content for any assignment in this course
units.policy: Using an artificial intelligence program to generate any content for any assignment in this course (including examinations, papers, homework, and creative work) is not permitted.

units.why: The template says such use "constitutes plagiarism and is a violation of the Honor Code", classifying AI generation as misconduct handled by the integrity process, so P36.
units.anchor: constitutes plagiarism and is a violation of the Honor Code

units.why: The template adds that use "without permission from the instructor may also constitute seeking unauthorized assistance"; this is another misconduct classification (P36) and implies instructor permission can authorize use, but its main job is the integrity classification.
units.anchor: without permission from the instructor may also constitute seeking unauthorized assistance

units.why: "Any suspicion of academic misconduct will be reported to the Honor Council" is a mandatory enforcement step in the template, so P36 (handled by integrity processes) with a must modality.
units.anchor: Any suspicion of academic misconduct will be reported to the Honor Council.

documents.title: Considerations for Detection: Artificial Intelligence
documents.stance_why: The sheet sets no rule on whether students may use AI; it advises faculty on evidence for "unauthorized or unattributed use of a GenAI program", which presupposes that authorization is set elsewhere (by instructors), so it is coded delegates.
documents.summary: A short Honor Council sheet on detecting AI misuse. It cautions about AI detectors and lists indicators of generative AI use that faculty can look for, and it points to a holistic review that includes asking the student about their work. It does not itself say whether AI is permitted.

units.why: "Emory does not currently license an AI detection program" is a fact about institutional tooling that underlies the detection guidance; closest type is P39 (detectors not relied upon), as no detector is provided.
units.anchor: Emory does not currently license an AI detection program.

units.why: It says "not a solid consensus" on detector accuracy, an explanation of why detectors are doubtful; P39 (detectors unreliable).
units.anchor: There is not a solid consensus in the educational and academic integrity communities

units.why: "Detection programs may produce false negatives or false positives" states unreliability, P39.
units.anchor: Detection programs may produce false negatives or false positives.

units.why: Detector results "alone would not ordinarily be sufficient" for a finding of responsibility, so detectors cannot be sole proof; P39.
units.anchor: would not ordinarily be sufficient to find a student responsible for a violation

units.why: Faculty using detectors "should be transparent and ask students to acknowledge in writing"; this is faculty disclosure of their own AI-tool use to students, P47 rather than P39 because it concerns disclosure, not reliability.
units.anchor: should be transparent and ask students to acknowledge in writing

units.why: Faculty "should exclude the student's name or other personally identifiable information from submission" is a data-protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: Faculty should exclude the student’s name or other personally identifiable information from submission.

units.why: "Faculty should treat these results with caution" repeats the unreliability theme as advice, P39.
units.anchor: Faculty should treat these results with caution.

units.why: Hallucinations are called "one of the most obvious signs of GenAI usage", an indicator for identifying misuse by process evidence, so P40.
units.anchor: These are one of the most obvious signs of GenAI usage.

units.why: Fabricated quotations or citations "may also be an honor code violation in and of itself", classifying hallucinated citations as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: may also be an honor code violation in and of itself

units.why: A paper containing a phrase like "Is there anything else I can help you with?" is a direct sign of AI generation, an indicator for P40.
units.anchor: Direct signs that the work was generated by AI

units.why: "Writing style that is markedly different from the student's previous work" is a stated indicator used to identify misuse, P40.
units.anchor: Writing style that is markedly different from the student’s previous work.

units.why: Writing "vastly different from the class or the expectations for undergraduates" is another indicator, P40.
units.anchor: Writing that is vastly different from the class or the expectations for undergraduates.

units.why: Grammar or vocabulary "beyond the course level (for languages)" is an indicator of AI use, P40.
units.anchor: Advanced grammatical structures or vocabulary that is beyond the course level

units.why: "Inclusion of material that is not germane to the course" is listed as an indicator, P40.
units.anchor: Inclusion of material that is not germane to the course.

units.why: Instructors can submit the assignment to a GenAI program and compare; "Work that is very similar to known GenAI output" is an indicator, a process-evidence check, P40.
units.anchor: Work that is very similar to known GenAI output.

units.why: "Student's inability to discuss their own work" is an indicator; P40 fits (evidence of misuse), while P30 is about students' duty to explain, which this does not state directly.
units.anchor: Student’s inability to discuss their own work.

units.why: "The honor code allows faculty to ask a student questions about their work" to clarify suspicion, i.e. talking with the student before escalating, P57.
units.anchor: allows faculty to ask a student questions about their work

units.why: The Council "advocates for a holistic approach" using course context and previous work to judge whether use was "unauthorized or unattributed"; this is weighing multiple evidence, P40, while P36 is secondary.
units.anchor: advocates for a holistic approach in determining whether an assignment may violate the honor code
units.frag_end: full picture for the Honor Council.

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) policy page
documents.stance_why: The page says "It is important to clearly state whether any use of AI is permitted or not" and gives guidance for both the no-AI and the permitted case, so it leaves the stance to instructors and is coded delegates.
documents.summary: A Learning Design policy page on AI for Emory College online courses. It defines AI and generative AI, notes concerns, repeats the Honor Council no-AI template, and offers advice for instructors who permit AI. It asks instructors to state clearly whether AI is allowed.

units.why: "Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the use of computer systems to simulate human processes" is a definition setting scope, P61.
units.anchor: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the use of computer systems to simulate human processes.

units.why: The definition of generative AI as models that "produce content in various forms" is a second definition of scope, P61.
units.anchor: Generative AI is a form of artificial intelligence that
units.policy: Generative AI is a form of artificial intelligence that uses machine learning models to produce content in various forms, including text, images, sounds, animations, and other types of data, often in response to prompts.

units.why: "concerns relate to academic integrity, ethics, access, and bias" names ethical, access and bias concerns about AI, P53 (the closest type, covering ethics and bias).
units.anchor: concerns relate to academic integrity, ethics, access, and bias

units.why: "It is important to clearly state whether any use of AI is permitted or not" tells instructors to state their AI rule, P09.
units.anchor: It is important to clearly state whether any use of AI is permitted or not.

units.why: The Honor Council language bars using AI "to generate any content for any assignment in this course", a no-AI default for graded work in the suggested syllabus text, P01.
units.anchor: Using an artificial intelligence program to generate any content for any assignment
units.policy: Using an artificial intelligence program to generate any content for any assignment in this course (including examinations, papers, homework, and creative work) is not permitted.

units.why: The language states such use "constitutes plagiarism and is a violation of the Honor Code", P36.
units.anchor: constitutes plagiarism and is a violation of the Honor Code

units.why: Use "without permission from the instructor may also constitute seeking unauthorized assistance" is a misconduct classification, P36.
units.anchor: without permission from the instructor may also constitute seeking unauthorized assistance

units.why: "Any suspicion of academic misconduct will be reported to the Honor Council" is a required enforcement step, P36.
units.anchor: Any suspicion of academic misconduct will be reported to the Honor Council.

units.why: Advising instructors to "Generate responses to your own assignments" to see what AI would produce is an instructor use of AI in preparing a course, P59, and not a redesign (P35).
units.anchor: Generate responses to your own assignments to see what an AI response might look like.

units.why: "Be very clear about your expectations for when students can use it and when they cannot" asks permitting instructors to communicate rules, P09.
units.anchor: Be very clear about your expectations for when students can use it

units.why: "Have students turn in the original AI generated work along with their edited work" asks for submission of AI output and edits for permitted use; P26 (submit drafts/outputs) fits better than P35 because the point is evidence of the student's own editing.
units.anchor: turn in the original AI generated work along with their edited work.
units.policy: Ask students to submit work generated by AI and demonstrate how they edited or adapted it, turning in the original AI generated work along with their edited work.

notes: Coder A. No university-wide or computing-unit policy found; all three included documents are Emory College (school layer). The three documents repeat the same Honor Council no-AI template; each was coded on its own. Some source text contains ligature characters, copied exactly in anchors.
